chief_complaint: progressive fatigue, pale skin, and dark tarry stools for 2 weeks
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, pale skin, and dark tarry stools for 2 weeks. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her dark bowel movements are simply from iron supplements and prune juice she took, and that her fatigue is just from overexertion.
concerns: She is worried that her extreme exhaustion and dizziness mean she will be too weak to look after her young grandson this weekend.
expectations: She hopes to get a blood booster injection or prescription iron tablets to quickly restore her energy levels.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (NSAID-Induced Gastric Ulcer) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (NSAID-Induced Gastric Ulcer) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes admitting the patient and checking CBC with type and cross, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive fatigue, pale skin, and dark tarry stools for 2 weeks

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, pale skin, and dark tarry stools for 2 weeks. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding (NSAID-Induced Gastric Ulcer).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Variceal haemorrhage without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Progressive fatigue and pallor over two weeks — suggests significant chronic blood loss and anaemia.
management_principles: Assess hemodynamic stability, secure IV access, admit, check CBC, type and cross
Hold NSAIDs, start high-dose IV PPI, schedule EGD
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of progressive fatigue, pale skin, and dark tarry stools for 2 weeks. HPI: NSAID-induced gastric ulcer bleeding.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding.
reference_soap.plan: Assess hemodynamic stability (vital signs, orthostatics) and secure IV access; transfuse packed red cells if indicated. Admit, check CBC with type and cross. Hold NSAIDs, start high-dose IV PPI, and schedule EGD within 24 hours. Consult gastroenterology and counsel the patient on NSAID avoidance.

teaching.one_liner: An NSAID-damaged ulcer in the stomach bleeds slowly over days, causing progressive fatigue, pale skin from anaemia, and black, tarry stools.
red_flags: Progressive fatigue and pallor over two weeks — suggests significant chronic blood loss and anaemia

must_ask.say: Can you describe the stool — is it black, tarry, and sticky?
How often do you take painkillers like ibuprofen?

Have you vomited any blood, or anything like coffee grounds?
Do you have any pain in your upper stomach area?

history.answer: I've been feeling completely exhausted lately, and for the past two weeks my bowel movements have looked pitch black and tarry.
It feels like a total lack of energy and general body heaviness rather than sleepiness. Even walking up a single flight of stairs wipes me out completely.
It started about two weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse each day. There was no specific sudden event that brought it on.
I have had to put off my usual daily chores because I just feel drained. Resting helps a tiny bit, but the deep tiredness never really goes away.
I feel worn out and weak all day long from the moment I wake up. It doesn't seem noticeably better or worse at any specific hour.
I sleep about seven to eight hours each night without waking up often. My husband says I do not snore, and I never stop breathing in my sleep.
My mood is fine, aside from being frustrated by having no energy. I am not feeling depressed, and I certainly have no thoughts of harming myself.
Yes, I feel quite dizzy and lightheaded whenever I stand up too quickly. It feels like my vision dims for a few seconds before clearing.
My stools have been sticky, foul-smelling, and jet black like wet coal for about two weeks. I haven't seen any bright red blood.
I went through menopause over ten years ago when I was fifty. I have not had any vaginal bleeding or spotting since then.
No, I haven't had any unusual bruises appearing on my skin, and my gums do not bleed when I brush my teeth.
No, I haven't felt any numbness, tingling, or pins-and-needles sensations in my hands or feet.
No, I have not become unusually sensitive to the cold, and my weight has not gone up. My skin feels normal, not particularly dry.
No, I haven't been excessively thirsty, and I am not urinating more often than usual.
My skin has looked noticeably paler, but not darker or bronzed. My appetite has been slightly lower, but I still eat regular meals.
No, I don't have any itchy skin, and my sense of taste is normal. My urine output and appearance have been typical.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats. My weight has stayed completely steady.
I get out of breath if I walk quickly or climb the stairs, though my breathing is fine at rest. My ankles and legs have not swollen at all.
history.topic: Shortness of breath and leg swelling

history.answer: I am retired, so my day-to-day life is quite peaceful without much stress. I have one cup of coffee in the morning and drink very little alcohol.
No, I haven't thrown up at all, and I have never vomited blood or anything looking like dark coffee grounds.
I've had a dull, gnawing ache in the pit of my stomach for a few weeks, which often feels worse when my stomach is empty.
No, I have never been diagnosed with a stomach ulcer or had any gastrointestinal bleeding in the past.
I've been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen four hundred milligrams almost every day for the past month because my right knee was aching.
I have been generally healthy without any history of high blood pressure, diabetes, liver trouble, or kidney disease.
I had my appendix removed when I was twenty-two, but I haven't had any other operations or hospital stays.
I do not take any prescription medications. Aside from the daily ibuprofen for my knee, I only take a standard daily multivitamin.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only have a glass of wine once or twice a month at family gatherings. I don't drink regularly.
I am a retired middle school teacher, and I live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no history of stomach cancer, colon cancer, anemia, or bleeding disorders in my family.
I thought my dark bowel movements were just from some prune juice and iron pills I took, and that I'm just run down from overworking myself.
I'm afraid that feeling this dizzy and exhausted means I won't be strong enough to babysit my grandson this weekend.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and temperature 36.8°C.
Standing blood pressure drops to 96/60 mmHg with an increase in heart rate to 112 beats/min.
The patient appears fatigued and noticeably pale, but is alert, oriented, and in no acute distress.
Marked pallor of the palpebral conjunctivae bilaterally; sclerae are clear and anicteric.
No palpable lymphadenopathy in the cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular chains.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and consistency, without tenderness or palpable nodules.
Regular tachycardia with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs detected.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on deep palpation in the epigastric region; no guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
Dark, tarry black stool is present on the examining glove; no anal fissures, hemorrhoids, or masses.
No pitting edema or swelling in either lower extremity.
